From one statement to a card shared by two companies

How this skill checks a company card against your books, shown one level at a time, from a statement that ties on the first pass up to a card paying another company's bills. Every rule is quoted from the skill itself, and every number is worked through in front of you.

The rules are the skill's ownEach one is quoted with the step it comes from, so you can read it yourself.
Each rule is backed by an authorityThe IRS, HMRC, the US consumer-finance regulator, the fraud examiners' association, the IFRS Foundation and QuickBooks' own documentation, numbered and linked.
The math is shownOpen "Check it yourself" on any level and follow every line on a calculator.
Your numbers, your checkAt the end, put in your own statement and watch the same rules run.

How it thinks

Five rules the whole skill runs on

Everything on this page is one of these rules applied to a bigger situation. The examples use one company, Northbrook Trading, one corporate card held by Dana Reyes, and the September statement.

Learning path

Seven levels, from simple to complex

Check it yourself

Put in your own statement

One card, one statement period, or load one of the levels above. The page builds the tie-out, counts the receipt exceptions against your threshold, and tests one purchase against your capitalisation line. Nothing is sent anywhere.

From the statement
From your books
Receipts and thresholds

The tie-out is the skill's Step 2 bridge. The receipt categories (matched, below threshold, missing) are the skill's Step 3; your threshold is yours, and the IRS's own line is $75 for most expenses1. The capital test compares one purchase with your threshold; the IRS safe harbor is $2,500 per item without audited statements3.

Where every fact on this page comes from

Rules are the skill's own. Facts below come from tax authorities, a regulator, a professional association, a standard-setter and the accounting software's own documentation, as published when checked on 22 October 2026. Follow the link for today's wording.

    Not backed by an outside authority: the receipt-status categories, the three monthly tests and the "review, not reconciliation" labelling are the skill's own rules. The page marks them as the skill's where they appear.

    Using it

    What it asks, needs and gives back

    Asks firstMosoFin as the data source, or upload? Which card and whose? Which statement period, and does it match your month? The statement and receipts. Your receipt and capitalisation thresholds. Can you reclaim tax?
    NeedsYour books' card charges and liability balance, connected or exported, plus the statement and the receipts, which only you can supply.
    Gives backThe tie-out, every charge with its receipt status, exceptions by severity with the three monthly tests, proposed entries in your account names, and a coverage sheet naming what it could not check.
    NeverPosts, pays the card, calls a review a reconciliation, treats an attached file as a matched receipt, or names an employee on test data. It reads nothing before you say yes.
    Rules are quoted from the skill's own reference files: references/overview.md on what a connected workspace gives you, references/method.md Steps 2 to 6 and Both entity scenarios, and references/edge-cases.md. Facts are cited to the sources above. All dollar figures are worked examples, not your data. The receipt, capitalisation and dispute rules cited are US ones and the tax-invoice rule is a UK one; confirm with your accountant what applies to you.
